queseq3-kmethod#62.en: k is a stand-in. Swap the bracket back in and keep solving.

queseq3-kmethod#63.en: Rule of thumb: the equation's highest power is x⁴. AT MOST how many real solutions?

queseq3-kmethod#64.en: The highest power tells you the maximum: x⁴ → up to 4 real solutions (equal roots count as one value).

queseq3-kmethod#65.en: Fully factorised, an equation splits into one bracket per power

queseq3-kmethod#66.en: x⁴ means four brackets, and each one can give at most one x-value

queseq3-kmethod#68.en: fewer if some are non-real or repeat

queseq3-kmethod#69.en: Rule of thumb: the equation's highest power is x². AT MOST how many real solutions?

queseq3-kmethod#70.en: A square → up to 2 real solutions.

queseq3-kmethod#71.en: x² means two brackets, so at most two x-values

queseq3-kmethod#73.en: Δ decides whether you get two, one or none

queseq3-kmethod#74.en: Rule of thumb: the equation's highest power is x³. AT MOST how many real solutions?

queseq3-kmethod#75.en: A cube → up to 3 real solutions.

queseq3-kmethod#76.en: x³ means three brackets, so at most three x-values

queseq3-kmethod#78.en: Solving gives x = 2, x = 2 and x = −1. How many DIFFERENT solutions is that?

queseq3-kmethod#79.en: 2 — equal roots count as ONE value

queseq3-kmethod#83.en: x = 2 twice is still just the value 2. Different solutions: x = 2 and x = −1 — two of them.

queseq3-kmethod#84.en: List the values you actually got: 2, 2 and −1

queseq3-kmethod#85.en: The question asks how many are DIFFERENT, and 2 written twice is still the single value 2

queseq3-kmethod#86.en: ∴ two different solutions: x = 2 and x = −1

queseq3-kmethod#87.en: a repeated root counts once — equal roots

queseq3-kmethod#88.en: Highest power = the most real answers you can expect; a repeated answer counts once.

queseq3-kmethod#89.en: The equation contains (y² − 2y)² … and later the terms −2y² + 4y. Where is the second copy of the bracket?

queseq3-kmethod#90.en: −2y² + 4y = −2(y² − 2y) — factor out −2 and the repeat appears

queseq3-kmethod#91.en: There is no second copy — the k-method can't be used

queseq3-kmethod#93.en: Swap it to 4y − 2y² and it becomes the bracket

queseq3-kmethod#94.en: Take out the common factor −2: −2y² + 4y = −2(y² − 2y). Now (y² − 2y) appears twice, so let k = y² − 2y.

queseq3-kmethod#95.en: Before deciding an equation has no repeated bracket, what should you try?

queseq3-kmethod#96.en: Factor a constant out of the loose terms — the repeat often hides behind a −2 or a 3

queseq3-kmethod#99.en: Take the square root of every term

queseq3-kmethod#100.en: A repeated expression often hides behind a common factor: −2y² + 4y hides (y² − 2y). Factor constants out FIRST, then look again.

queseq3-kmethod#101.en: Factor a number out of the loose x-terms and compare with the bracket.

queseq3-kmethod#102.en: The original equation had the repeated bracket in a DENOMINATOR, with restriction (bracket) ≠ ${C(r)}. Does the restriction carry over to k?

queseq3-kmethod#104.en: Yes — k stands for that bracket, so k ≠ ${C(r)} rides along. If solving gives k = ${C(r)}, reject it (N.A.).

queseq3-kmethod#105.en: k is not a new quantity — it is just a short name for that bracket

queseq3-kmethod#106.en: So anything true of the bracket is true of k, including (bracket) ≠ ${C(r)}

queseq3-kmethod#107.en: ∴ k ≠ ${C(r)} rides along, and a k-value of ${C(r)} would have to be rejected as N.A.

queseq3-kmethod#108.en: While using the k-method you find k = ${C(r)}, but the restriction was k ≠ ${C(r)}. What do you do?

queseq3-kmethod#109.en: Reject k = ${C(r)} (mark it N.A.) and keep only the other k-value

queseq3-kmethod#110.en: Keep it — restrictions are about x, not k

queseq3-kmethod#112.en: Start over with a different letter

queseq3-kmethod#113.en: A value that breaks a restriction is not applicable — cross it out with N.A. and continue with the surviving k-value.

queseq3-kmethod#114.en: The restriction says the bracket may not be ${C(r)}, and k IS the bracket

queseq3-kmethod#115.en: So k = ${C(r)} would make a denominator 0 — it cannot be used

queseq3-kmethod#116.en: Mark it N.A. with a struck equals and carry on with the other k-value only

queseq3-kmethod#117.en: the restriction was set before solving, and it still holds afterwards

queseq3-kmethod#118.en: k inherits everything the bracket had — including its restriction.
